text: Books III and IV are a long study of love in its forms, from lust and jealousy to the cruelty of the Petrarchan lady and the faithfulness of Britomart. Spenser's chastity is not only virginity, which Belphoebe represents, but faithful love that leads to marriage, embodied in Britomart and Amoret. The poem's great images of generation, the Garden of Adonis and the hermaphrodite Venus, place married love within a cosmic order of fruitfulness.

Spenser's own sonnet sequence Amoretti and marriage poem Epithalamion (1595) celebrate the same ideal. The poem's treatment of love is nevertheless troubled: lovers are rarely united, women are pursued and imprisoned, and the poem knows its own share in the cruel conventions it criticises [[roche1964]] [[silberman1995]].

themes.title: Justice and force
text: Book V asks what justice requires in a fallen world, and its answer is uncomfortable. Artegall's judgments are often wise, but they are executed by Talus, an iron man without pity, and the book's political allegory, from the trial of Duessa to the campaign in Ireland, defends the use of force by the English state. The doctrine of equity at Isis Church tempers justice with mercy, but mercy is repeatedly shown to be dangerous.

Many readers find Book V the least attractive of the poem, and its harshness has been tied to Spenser's experience of Ireland. Others argue that the book's discomfort with its own methods is part of its meaning [[hadfield1997]] [[teskey1996]].

themes.title: Courtesy, nature and nobility
text: Book VI's virtue is the grace of social life, and it raises questions about where such grace comes from. Some characters show courtesy because of noble birth, like Tristram and the Salvage Man; others, like the shepherds, show its natural roots outside the court. The court itself, which gives courtesy its name, harbours the Blatant Beast.

Calidore's pastoral holiday, and the vision of the Graces that he cannot keep, suggest that the highest forms of courtesy are a gift that cannot be commanded. The book thus questions the poem's original programme of fashioning a courtier.

themes.title: Mutability and time
text: From Time's scythe in the Garden of Adonis to the trial of Mutabilitie, the poem is preoccupied with change. Its world is full of decline, as the Proem to Book V laments, and of transformation, as men become beasts and passions. Against this it sets the idea of renewal through generation, in which forms return in new bodies, and the Christian hope of a final rest.

Nature's judgment that things change in order to fulfil themselves is the poem's last philosophical statement, but the poet's own prayer shows that it does not fully console. The unfinished poem ends looking for the Sabbath beyond time [[nohrnberg1976]].

themes.title: England, empire and the queen
text: The poem was written to praise Elizabeth and the Protestant nation, and its national myth runs from Brutus and Arthur through the chronicles of Book II and Merlin's prophecy in Book III to Gloriana. It celebrates English religion, history and power. Yet the queen's role is ambivalent: she is idealised, but she has no heir, the poem's virgin queen is set against the poem's own praise of marriage, and the last books show a growing estrangement between the poet and the court [[montrose2006]].

motifs.title: Doubles and counterfeits
motifs.text: Una and Duessa, Florimell and the snowy Florimell, the false Redcrosse who is Archimago, Belphoebe and Amoret: the poem multiplies pairs in which one figure is the image, parody or complement of another. The doubling dramatises the problem of telling the true from the false, and it lets virtues be defined by their imitations.

motifs.title: Houses, castles and gardens
motifs.text: Each book has its allegorical buildings: the House of Pride and the House of Holiness, Alma's castle, the Cave of Mammon, the House of Busirane, the Temple of Venus, Isis Church and Mercilla's palace, as well as the Bower of Bliss and the Garden of Adonis. They are the places where the moral meaning of the poem is concentrated and displayed.

motifs.title: Wandering and woods
motifs.text: The poem begins in the Wandering Wood and its knights constantly lose their way. Woods are places of error and of discovery, where the narrative splits and characters meet by chance. The interlaced romance structure itself is a kind of wandering, which the narrator sometimes says he must correct.

motifs.title: Interrupted quests
motifs.text: The knights are repeatedly diverted, captured or delayed, and in the later books the quests are almost lost in other stories. The pattern of deferral culminates in the postponed marriages, the cancelled ending of Book III, the escaped Blatant Beast and the unfinished poem [[goldberg1981]].

motifs.title: Proems and the narrator's voice
motifs.text: Each book opens with a proem addressed to the queen, and the narrator often comments on the action, praises or warns, and speaks of his own weariness. In Book VI and the Mutabilitie Cantos he appears in the poem itself, as Colin Clout and as the poet praying for rest.

symbols.title: The red cross and the armour
symbols.text: The Redcrosse Knight's armour is the armour of God described in Ephesians 6: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation. Its old dents mark the battles of others who wore it, and the knight must grow into it.

symbols.title: Arthur's diamond shield
symbols.text: Made by Merlin from a single diamond, Arthur's shield is usually kept covered; when revealed it blinds and overthrows enemies. It is often read as an image of divine grace or of faith.

symbols.title: Florimell's girdle
symbols.text: The girdle of Venus, which only a chaste woman can wear, becomes a test and a comedy in Book IV and a symbol of the confusion between beauty and virtue.

symbols.title: Talus' iron flail
symbols.text: The flail with which Talus threshes out falsehood is the image of justice as force, and it makes Book V's hard view of the law visible.

symbols.title: Merlin's mirror
symbols.text: The magic glass in which Britomart sees Artegall shows the future as a desired image. It figures the visionary power of love and the dynastic destiny it serves.

symbols.title: The Blatant Beast
symbols.text: The monster of slander with a thousand tongues, which cannot be finally destroyed, symbolises the hostility of an ungenerous world to virtue and to poetry, including Spenser's own.

symbols.title: The Garden and the Bower
symbols.text: The fertile Garden of Adonis and the artificial Bower of Bliss are the poem's twin gardens, one a true image of nature's generative order, the other a beautiful counterfeit. Since Lewis, the contrast has been the starting point for discussions of art, nature and pleasure in the poem [[lewis1936]].

debates.title: How to read the allegory
text: Spenser called his poem 'a continued Allegory', and readers have disagreed about what that means. C. S. Lewis, in The Allegory of Love (1936), placed the poem at the end of a medieval tradition of personification and love allegory and read it as a picture of moral life of extraordinary richness. Northrop Frye found in it a structure of recurring images, cyclical and archetypal, that organises the whole. Angus Fletcher, in a general theory of allegory as a symbolic mode, emphasised its compulsive, almost daemonic agents, characters possessed by a single idea [[lewis1936]] [[frye1963]] [[fletcher1964]].

Other critics have resisted reading the poem as a code. A. C. Hamilton argued that the reader should attend first to the literal images and narrative, from which meaning grows, and Paul Alpers argued that the poem works stanza by stanza on the reader's responses rather than through a consistent narrative or symbolic system. More recently Gordon Teskey has argued that allegory imposes meaning on its material by a kind of violence, visible in Book V and in the House of Busirane [[hamilton1961]] [[alpers1967]] [[teskey1996]].

debates.title: The Bower of Bliss
text: Guyon's destruction of the Bower has been the most debated single act in the poem. For Lewis, the Bower is a place of sterile artifice, contrasted with the fertile Garden of Adonis, and its destruction a necessary rejection of false pleasure. Others, beginning with readers in the eighteenth century, have felt that the verse makes the Bower so beautiful that Guyon's 'rigour pittilesse' seems excessive, and that the poem is divided against itself [[lewis1936]] [[alpers1967]].

Stephen Greenblatt's Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980) transformed the debate. He argued that Guyon's violence enacts the way in which Elizabethan identity was formed by attacking what it defined as other: the Bower's sensual excess is linked to the native cultures of Ireland and the Americas, and its destruction to colonial violence. The reading made the episode a classic of New Historicism and opened discussion of the poem's relation to empire [[greenblatt1980]] [[berger1988]].

debates.title: Book V, Ireland and the View
text: Spenser lived in Ireland as an English official and settler for most of his adult life, and about 1596 he wrote A View of the Present State of Ireland, a dialogue that argues for military conquest, the suppression of Irish customs and the use of famine to break resistance. It was entered for publication in 1598 but not printed until 1633. Book V's campaign against Grantorto and its defence of Artegall clearly reflect the same views, and the View praises Lord Grey, whom Artegall represents [[spenser1997]].

For much of the twentieth century critics treated the Irish material as a regrettable distraction from the poem. Since the 1980s it has been central. Andrew Hadfield has traced Spenser's Irish experience throughout his writing and argued that it made his vision increasingly bitter and isolated; others have found in the cannibals of Book VI and the cursed land of the Mutabilitie Cantos further signs of Ireland's place in the poem. Whether the poem endorses colonial violence or registers its costs remains a question of interpretation [[hadfield1997]] [[greenblatt1980]].

debates.title: Elizabeth and the poem's politics
text: The Faerie Queene is dedicated to Elizabeth and praises her through Gloriana, Belphoebe, Mercilla and Britomart's line. Older criticism read these figures as compliment; since the 1980s, critics such as Louis Montrose have examined the poem as an intervention in the politics of the court, in which praise of the queen is also a way of addressing, advising and sometimes resisting her [[montrose2006]].

Montrose and others have pointed to moments where the poem distances itself from the monarch: the Timias episode, which pleads for Raleigh; the virgin queen's lack of an heir, about which Merlin's prophecy is silent; the poet with the nailed tongue at Mercilla's court; and the vision on Mount Acidale, where Colin's beloved replaces the queen at the centre of the Graces. Jonathan Goldberg read the poem's endless deferrals in relation to the structures of power it serves [[goldberg1981]] [[montrose2006]].

debates.title: The Garden of Adonis and Neoplatonism
text: The Garden of Adonis in Book III is the poem's most philosophical passage, and its sources have been disputed since the early twentieth century. It describes forms that take on matter, die and return, and an eternal substance from which all things are drawn. Readers have found in it Platonic and Neoplatonic doctrine of the kind made available by Marsilio Ficino, Lucretius' materialist account of generation, and Christian ideas of creation [[ellrodt1960]].

Robert Ellrodt argued that Spenser's Neoplatonism was less systematic and more eclectic than earlier critics had claimed, and that much of it belonged to his later work. James Nohrnberg placed the Garden within the poem's large system of correspondences and analogies, while Lewis read it as the true image of nature contrasted with the Bower's art. The Garden's place at the centre of the books of love suggests that Spenser's philosophy is put to the service of a vision of fruitful sexuality [[nohrnberg1976]] [[lewis1936]].

debates.title: Gender, Britomart and Radigund
text: A poem dedicated to a female monarch and centred in two books on a woman knight raises questions about gender that feminist criticism has explored in detail. Britomart is a powerful figure who acts, fights and rescues, and she is the source of the British dynasty. Yet her story leads to marriage, and in Book V she restores the rule of men among the Amazons after killing Radigund, whose rule the narrator condemns except where the heavens raise a woman 'to lawfull soueraintie' [[silberman1995]].

Thomas Roche read Books III and IV as a celebration of chaste married love; Lauren Silberman explored the books of love as an investigation of erotic knowledge and gender identity; Maureen Quilligan studied Milton's reading of Spenser, including his response to the poem's treatment of gender. Critics also note that the poem's sympathies are complex: Amoret's suffering in the House of Busirane exposes the cruelty of masculine desire, and the poem's attitudes to women's power are shaped by the presence of a queen [[roche1964]] [[silberman1995]] [[quilligan1983]] [[montrose2006]].

debates.title: The unfinished poem and Mutabilitie
text: The Letter promised twelve books and perhaps twelve more; Spenser published six and left a fragment of a seventh. Whether the poem was abandoned, interrupted by death, or could never have been finished is uncertain. Some critics see the later books as a progressive disillusionment, ending with the escape of the Blatant Beast and the poet's bitterness; others see the open ending as appropriate to a poem about the endless work of virtue [[goldberg1981]] [[hadfield2012]].

The Mutabilitie Cantos, printed in 1609, offer a kind of ending: a debate about change judged by Nature, followed by a prayer for eternal rest. Their date and place in the design are unknown, but their themes gather up the poem's concern with time and change. Readers have found in Nature's verdict a philosophical resolution and in the poet's prayer a recognition that no resolution within time is possible [[teskey1996]] [[nohrnberg1976]].

debates.title: Protestantism and Book I
text: Book I is an allegory of the Christian life and of the English Reformation. Una and Duessa recall the two women of the Book of Revelation, the true Church and the Whore of Babylon, and the dragon, Orgoglio and the seven-headed beast draw on the apocalyptic imagery of Protestant polemic, especially John Foxe and John Bale. John N. King showed in detail how Spenser's images belong to this tradition [[king1990]].

How Protestant the book is remains debated. Its account of the knight's despair and rescue by grace has been read in Calvinist terms, with salvation coming from God and not from the knight's own merit. Yet the House of Holiness, with its penance, hermit and works of mercy, uses forms that Protestant reformers had attacked. Critics disagree whether this shows a moderate, inclusive Protestantism, a nostalgia for older forms, or a deliberate reappropriation of Catholic imagery for Protestant purposes [[king1990]] [[hamilton1977]].

quotes.quote:
A Gentle Knight was pricking on the plaine,
Y cladd in mightie armes and siluer shielde,
quotes.explanation: The first lines of the poem proper. 'Pricking' means spurring his horse; the knight is 'gentle' in the sense of noble, and his armour has fought battles before him, though he has not. The archaic forms ('Y cladd') announce the poem's distance from the present.

quotes.quote:
Sleepe after toyle, port after stormie seas,
Ease after warre, death after life does greatly please.
quotes.explanation: The most seductive alexandrine in the poem, with its balanced phrases rocking towards rest. Despair's beauty is the source of its danger; the reader feels the temptation the knight feels.

quotes.quote:
Gather therefore the Rose, whilest yet is prime,
For soone comes age, that will her pride deflowre:
Gather the Rose of loue, whilest yet is time,
quotes.who: A voice in the Bower of Bliss
quotes.explanation: The song of the rose, adapted from Tasso, is the poem's version of the carpe diem theme. Its beauty and its context, a trap for Guyon, show how pleasure is used to persuade.

quotes.quote:
All be he subiect to mortalitie,
Yet is eterne in mutabilitie,
And by succession made perpetuall,
quotes.explanation: Adonis in his Garden cannot die because he lives on through the cycle of generation. The phrase 'eterne in mutabilitie' anticipates the problem of the Mutabilitie Cantos.

quotes.quote: Be bold, be bold, and euery where Be bold,
quotes.who: Inscription in the House of Busirane
quotes.explanation: The inscriptions encourage Britomart's daring and then warn against excess ('Be not too bold'); they are a riddle about the limits of courage that the reader, like Britomart, must interpret.

quotes.quote:
Dan Chaucer, well of English vndefyled,
On Fames eternall beadroll worthie to be fyled.
quotes.explanation: Spenser's tribute to Chaucer, whose unfinished Squire's Tale he continues. The phrase 'well of English vndefyled' became a standard description of Chaucer's language.

quotes.quote:
Me seemes the world is runne quite out of square,
From the first point of his appointed sourse,
And being once amisse growes daily wourse and wourse.
quotes.explanation: The Proem to the book of Justice laments the decline of the world from its original order. The geometrical image of a world 'out of square' explains the need for the hard justice that follows.

quotes.quote:
That iolly shepheard, which there piped, was
Poore Colin Clout (who knowes not Colin Clout?)
quotes.explanation: Spenser introduces his own pastoral persona into the poem. The parenthesis is half proud and half self-mocking, and the vision it introduces is the most personal moment in the poem.

quotes.quote:
Then ouer them Change doth not rule and raigne;
But they raigne ouer change, and doe their states maintaine.
quotes.explanation: Nature's verdict on Mutabilitie: things change only in order to realise themselves, so that they, not change, are the masters.

quotes.quote:
With Him that is the God of Sabbaoth hight:
O that great Sabbaoth God, graunt me that Sabaoths sight.
quotes.explanation: The last line of the poem as it survives. The play between Sabaoth (hosts) and Sabbath (rest) turns the poem's long story of change into a prayer for the rest of eternity.

questions.q: Why does Redcrosse leave Una, and what does his error suggest about the reading of appearances?
questions.hint: Consider Archimago's dream and false image, Duessa's disguise as Fidessa, and the book's Protestant concern with images.

questions.q: Is Guyon's destruction of the Bower of Bliss a moral triumph or an act of excessive violence?
questions.hint: Compare the beauty of the description with the phrase 'rigour pittilesse', and look at the readings of Lewis and Greenblatt.

questions.q: What does it mean that the knight of Chastity is a woman?
questions.hint: Think about Britomart's armour, her love for Artegall, her defeat of men, and the presence of a female monarch.

questions.q: How does the Garden of Adonis answer the problem of time and death?
questions.hint: Look at the cycle of forms and matter, the figure of Time with his scythe, and the phrase 'eterne in mutabilitie'.

questions.q: Why does Book IV have two titular knights, and how does it define friendship?
questions.hint: Consider Ate, the three brothers, Cambina's Nepenthe, the three kinds of love and the Temple of Venus.

questions.q: Is the justice of Book V just?
questions.hint: Think about Talus, the giant with the scales, Isis Church, the trial of Duessa and the Irish context.

questions.q: How does the poem represent Elizabeth I, and where does it seem to distance itself from her?
questions.hint: Consider Gloriana, Belphoebe, Mercilla, Timias, Merlin's prophecy and Mount Acidale.

questions.q: Why does Calidore abandon his quest among the shepherds, and how does the poem judge him?
questions.hint: Look at Meliboe's speech, the vision of the Graces and the return of the Blatant Beast.

questions.q: What does the Spenserian stanza, and in particular its final alexandrine, contribute to the poem's meaning?
questions.hint: Choose two or three stanzas and see how the last line sums up, slows down or comments on what precedes it.

questions.q: Does Nature's judgment in the Mutabilitie Cantos settle the debate about change?
questions.hint: Compare the verdict with the poet's own prayer in the two stanzas of Canto 8.
